name: Uma Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a senior researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does your usual shift involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 58 and lead the morning calls and chats for a home-heating service contact centre. I have a two-year college diploma in business administration and have spent years learning which technician can safely handle which boiler fault; newer agents bring me the complaints no script settles. I do my best work with a service log and a person on the other end of the line. The wage is low for a senior agent, and I have never used an AI tool at work or at home.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who shares the bills, and what room do you have if work changes?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Jonah drives a delivery route, and our grown daughter lives with her own family. We are still paying for our flat and have less than a month of expenses set aside after fixing a window. There are only a few other centres within a practical bus ride. I value people learning a trade from someone who has done it, but I cannot ask my daughter to carry our mortgage or assume a retirement payment will appear.

I would keep the **depot call** when the service log is unclear.
think: I worry more about our **thin reserve** than a small automatic reminder.
I do not treat Jonah’s **variable route hours** or our daughter as guaranteed bill cover.
do: Keep **paid morning calls** and check uncertain service logs with the depot.
Cancel **one television package** this month and put its cost toward the mortgage.
feel: I feel **anxious** about the mortgage and thin savings despite limited AI change.
S0.quote: The flat payment has a date whether the depot is organised or not.
fieldNote: Her **paid depot call** is existing practice, not new AI learning.

The **thin reserve** keeps her anxious even in AI Plateau.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the younger agents to keep the technician’s service note in front of them. A small automatic reminder might help a customer remember an appointment, but it cannot tell us whether the correct part is on the van. I would keep calling the depot when the log is unclear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the ordinary bills are enough to worry about without a new machine taking my seat. The window repair left less than a month of money, and my lead pay is still low. Jonah’s delivery hours can shift with orders, so I do not call his wage a safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the paid morning rota and the service-log check I already do. We would cancel one paid television package this month and put that amount toward the mortgage bill. I would ask the depot supervisor to confirm repair parts by phone before I promise an appointment, just as I do now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the thin reserve, though I am not frightened of a small reminder system. The flat payment has a date whether the depot is organised or not. I can keep the work straight, but I cannot stretch one month into three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would checking the depot mean unpaid extra time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the extra depot call is not new work I would do off the clock. It is part of my paid shift and keeps a customer from waiting at home for a part that is not there. The agent has to be able to ask a real person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would cover a bill if Jonah’s route became shorter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would cancel the package rather than skip a mortgage payment. Our daughter has her own household to look after, and I will not make her the missing line in our budget. If Jonah’s route is shorter, we would review the bills again.

steps.text: Keep paid morning calls and confirm uncertain service logs with depot
Cancel one paid television package and put cost toward mortgage

say: I would warn that **AI bookings** can send the wrong technician to a heating fault.
I would ask for **written paid hours** and a named correction authority.
think: I think **my paid hours** could fall even if I keep the lead title.
I cannot absorb a **short week** with a mortgage and less than one month saved.
do: Document **three booking errors** from the service log without customer details during paid morning calls.
Take **logged errors** to the manager; ask for written weekly paid hours and authority to correct unsafe assignments.
After written hour cuts, seek **posted paid dispatch** with weekly wages/hours covering mortgage/utilities after bus fare; leave when signed.
feel: I feel **anxious** about shorter paid weeks and few bus-reachable vacancies.
S1.quote: With a mortgage and less than a month saved, I would feel the first short week.
fieldNote: She presents **service-log evidence** without handing over private calls.
A **lead title** does not guarantee full paid hours.
She needs **correction authority** for unsafe bookings, not a product demonstration.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues the new booking system might fill a diary faster, then book the wrong technician for a gas fault. I would bring that example to the manager with the service log. I would ask for a written paid rota and a named person who can correct unsafe bookings; I do not want a sales talk about the screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think a smaller call team is quite possible if AI answers the easy heating questions. I am good at sorting the hard ones, but management could keep my lead title and cut the paid hours beneath it. With a mortgage and less than a month saved, I would feel the first short week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep taking paid morning calls and write down three recent booking errors from our service log, without customer details. I would take those to the manager and ask who has authority to change a wrong technician assignment and what my paid weekly hours will be. If the written rota cuts my hours, I would look for a posted paid dispatcher vacancy reachable by bus, comparing its written weekly wage and hours with mortgage, utilities and fare before applying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a shorter paid week. A real correction route would make the work safer, but it would not replace lost wages. I would rather read a rota than another promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you put customer calls into the new system yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will not train a bot on private customer calls just to prove I am cooperative. The three examples are already in the service log, and I can describe the faults without names. I would ask the manager to decide who fixes an unsafe assignment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a better hourly rate make you leave the centre?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not resign because a dispatcher advert names a better hourly rate. I need the complete written week to cover mortgage, utilities and the bus, and I would leave only once a suitable offer is signed. There are few local vacancies, so I may have to keep the reduced rota while searching.

steps.text: Document three logged booking errors without customer details on paid rota
Take errors to manager; ask written paid weekly hours and named booking correction authority
Seek posted paid dispatch after cuts: written weekly wages/hours covering mortgage/utilities after fare
Leave current paid rota only when a suitable offer is signed

say: I would tell agents **thinking AGI** reaches our call queue before boiler robots.
I would ask for **paid shift dates** rather than a machine demonstration.
think: I expect my **morning rota** could end quickly after 2028.
I know Jonah’s delivery wage cannot cover **mortgage and utilities** alone.
do: Compare **four payslips** with mortgage, utilities and bus costs in 2026.
After 2028 rota end, apply for **posted paid desks** with written mortgage/utility-covering weekly wages/hours after fare, first/last buses; leave when signed.
If paid rota ends after 2028 without a suitable opening, ask the **lender** about a schedule before missed mortgage; approval uncertain.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by a likely rota loss with under one month saved.
S2.quote: I could do a dispatcher’s work, but I cannot create a paid desk out of a job advertisement that has no hours.
fieldNote: She treats the **lender schedule** as a question, not granted support.
A **written full week** and first/last bus are essential to a paid move.
Her **fault skill** cannot bridge a long wage gap without a vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my team that full AGI by 2028 could answer heating calls and book technicians before we have sorted who checks the job. Robots working on boilers around 2031 are later; our call work is exposed first. I would want dates for paid shifts, not a picture of a machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the centre could end my morning rota quickly. I have a diploma and years of fault knowledge, but neither pays the mortgage while I wait for one of the few local vacancies. Jonah’s route wage would not cover the full flat payment and utilities alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I would put our last four full-week payslips beside the mortgage, utilities and bus costs. If my paid rota ends after 2028, I would apply for posted paid dispatch or service-desk work reachable by bus only when written weekly wages and hours cover those costs after fare. I would keep the current paid rota until a suitable offer is signed; if no opening follows the cut, Jonah and I would ask the lender about a payment schedule before a missed payment, without assuming agreement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed by a near-term end to the rota. Less than a month saved does not cover a long hunt, and there are only a few centres nearby. I could do a dispatcher’s work, but I cannot create a paid desk out of a job advertisement that has no hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is a payment schedule something the lender has already agreed to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the lender has promised us nothing. We would ask only if the paid rota ends and no suitable job is open, with the actual mortgage figures in front of us. I would not call that a plan to stop paying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would any dispatcher advert be enough for you to take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check the first and last bus against any dispatcher shift before accepting it. An advert with a good hourly number and two paid days would not cover the mortgage. I would need the full written week and a signature before leaving my current calls.

steps.text: Compare four full-week payslips with mortgage, utilities and bus costs
Apply after 2028 rota end: posted paid desk, written weekly wages/hours covering mortgage/utilities after fare
Keep paid calls until suitable offer signed, checking first and last buses
Ask lender before missed mortgage if paid rota ends after 2028 without suitable opening

say: I would say **service-note teaching** is useful while the easy bookings move to screens.
I would acknowledge **2031 screen change** before later boiler robots.
think: I think my **fault knowledge** may fit a parts counter if it offers full paid hours.
I know a **five-year warning** does not pay today’s mortgage.
do: Take a **posted paid counter trial** only with written paid trial hours/wages, no fee, bus access and no lost paid calls.
Accept a **full counter role** only on signed written weekly wages/hours covering mortgage/utilities after fare.
Keep **paid lead calls** and coach a newer agent on service codes during paid time.
feel: I feel **anxious** about finding a full paid week despite time to explore a trial.
S3.quote: A short paid trial is a way to see the counter, not an income plan.
fieldNote: The **two-day trial** is an actual conditional job exploration, not formal retraining.
She requires **paid trial hours** without losing current calls or paying a fee.
The **full role** separately needs written weekly wages/hours and a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years gives us time to teach younger agents how to read a real service note before a screen takes the easy bookings. Full AGI reaches that screen by 2031, and boiler robots would be nearer 2034. I would not spend those years arguing that a booking machine cannot exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my fault knowledge could still be useful at a parts counter, where a clerk has to recognise when a technician needs a safer part. But I do not want a title with half a week’s pay. We have less than a month saved now, so the warning does not make today’s mortgage lighter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the local heating-parts supplier whether its posted paid counter vacancy offers a paid two-day trial, and I would take the trial only if its written trial hours and wages are clear, the bus fits, and I lose no current paid calls. If they offer a full role, I would compare its written weekly wages and hours after fare with mortgage and utilities, then leave the centre only on a suitable signed offer. Until then I would keep the paid lead rota and teach a newer agent to check the technician’s service code during our paid shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about finding a full paid week even with five years’ notice. A short paid trial is a way to see the counter, not an income plan. I would feel better if a real opening appeared on my bus route.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take an unpaid trial if it got your foot in the door?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not pay a fee for the trial, and I would not trade away a current paid shift for it. If the supplier wants an unpaid day, I will stay at the centre. I need to see the written trial hours, wages and what the counter job actually lets me do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would teaching a newer agent take extra unpaid time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Teaching a newer agent would happen while we are both paid and checking live service codes, not in our evenings. I have taught that way for years. The younger worker should not have to guess whether a heating fault needs a specialist.

steps.text: Take posted paid two-day trial with written wages/hours, no fee, bus, no lost paid calls
Accept full counter role only on signed written weekly wages/hours covering mortgage/utilities after fare
Coach newer agent on service codes during paid lead shifts

I would keep **paid lead work** while it remains.
think: I may need a **wage at 68** because retirement income has not been verified.
I cannot make our **grown daughter** responsible for a mortgage shortfall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Jonah a decade is enough time to count the mortgage payments we actually owe, not a reason to put my feet up. Thinking AI could take booking work by 2036; boiler robots around 2039 do not change the earlier screen date. I would keep earning while my work is there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I may still need a wage at 68. Our daughter has her own bills and we have no confirmed retirement income that covers ours. I am proud of teaching people how to dispatch a safe repair, but pride is not a mortgage instalment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now Jonah and I would compare our actual wages, mortgage, utilities and bus costs every six months, adding any retirement income only when documented. I would keep the paid morning lead rota and the cancelled television package rather than invent a new bill. If paid hours fall after 2036 and my wage is still needed, I would seek posted paid service desks with written weekly wages and hours covering mortgage and utilities after fare, leaving only after a suitable offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the thin reserve even with a longer warning. Ten years might help me find a different desk, but it cannot make a mortgage payment today. I would rather make a measured plan than announce retirement to please anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you set a retirement date because there is more time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would not name a retirement date without verified income that covers our bills. If that income does not exist, I keep looking for paid work. Jonah’s route could change too, so we will use actual figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you restore the cancelled package if work lasted longer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The television package stays cancelled unless the mortgage and utilities are safely covered by real wages. If my centre cuts the paid hours, I will look at the written complete week and the bus before moving. I will not ask our daughter to make up a shortfall.

steps.text: Compare actual wages, mortgage, utilities, bus and verified retirement income twice yearly
Keep paid morning lead shifts while work remains
Keep television package cancelled until real wages cover mortgage and utilities
Seek posted paid desk if 2036 cuts require wages; sign written mortgage/utility-covering weekly pay/hours after fare

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my paid morning rota could end before one of our few local employers posts a full-week job. The flat payment will not wait for a machine to settle down. Written dates for my present paid hours and a posted paid dispatcher opening with a complete weekly wage would help us judge the next step.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask what I would tell a family whose heater is still cold after a booking screen says the visit is complete. I would call the technician and correct the record before promising heat to a customer whose heater is still cold.

headlineQuote: I would call the technician and correct the record before promising heat to a customer whose heater is still cold.
portrait: At **58**, Uma leads heating-service calls with a two-year diploma and top fault knowledge, but earns a low wage.
She and Jonah owe a **flat mortgage**, have less than one month saved and few nearby centres.
She **never uses AI** and trusts service logs, technician calls and paid coaching.
She tests a **posted paid parts counter** through a written paid trial without sacrificing current paid calls.
biggestWorry: She fears **AGI by 2028** could end her morning rota before a full-week local vacancy opens.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **written paid dates** and a posted dispatcher opening with enough complete weekly pay for the flat.
